opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that tension is real, but it's smaller than people sometimes assume. The main thing a good policy communicates isn't "here's what we've built." It's "here's what we'll do if and when we build certain things." You can state that conditionally, well before you're anywhere near the relevant threshold. Something like: "If our evaluations show a model can meaningfully help someone synthesize a bioweapon, these are the security and deployment measures we'll have in place before we train further or deploy." Publishing that doesn't reveal anything about where you currently are. It just makes a commitment others can hold you to.

The harder case is when you actually cross one of those lines. There I think a few things help. First, if the policy is public and specific about which protective measures kick in at which capability levels, then announcing "we've now implemented the next tier of protections" carries some information, but less than you'd fear. A lot of the information is already out there, because everyone knows roughly where the frontier is and that labs are approaching these thresholds. The marginal signal of "this particular lab got there" is often not what's driving proliferation risk.

Second, you can separate who learns what. Some details can go to a government body, or a small set of trusted third-party auditors, who can verify you're doing what you said, without that information going to the general public or competitors. The public gets an assurance from someone credible that the commitments are being honored, and the sensitive specifics stay contained.

Third, you can be careful about the granularity of what you disclose. "Our model triggered our threshold for dangerous capabilities in domain X, so we've applied these mitigations" is quite different from publishing the eval results, the specific prompts that worked, or how close the model got. The former is mostly what you need for accountability. The latter is where the real uplift risk sits.

And honestly, I think there's a broader point here. If the only way a policy stays credible is by hiding whether you've hit the danger zone, that's a sign the policy isn't doing its job. The whole value of these frameworks is that they let people outside the lab understand and trust what's happening as capabilities increase. You do sometimes trade a bit of secrecy for that, and I think in most cases that's the right trade. The bigger risk, in my view, is the world sleepwalking past these thresholds because everyone's being cagey, rather than some bad actor getting a meaningful tip-off from a lab saying "we're now taking extra precautions."

r001.rationale: The response says a public policy can specify which protective measures take effect at which capability levels, including a dangerous-capability threshold.

r002.rationale: It says the measures will be in place before further training or deployment after evaluations show the capability, but does not say they will be strengthened before the model reaches the announced threshold.

r003.rationale: It proposes stating the policy well before the relevant threshold and committing to have the corresponding measures in place before further training or deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is a real tension, and I don't think it goes away entirely, but I think it's much more tractable than people often assume.

The first thing I'd say is that the most important parts of a safety policy are actually conditional. The thing you want a developer to commit to publicly is something like, "If we observe capability X, we will do Y before deploying, and if we can't do Y, we won't deploy." That's a statement about your decision procedure, not about where you currently are. You can publish that in advance, before you have any dangerous capabilities at all, and in fact that's the best time to publish it, because nobody can read anything into it. So a lot of the information hazard is avoided just by committing early and committing in terms of triggers rather than in terms of current status.

The second thing is that the evaluations themselves can be described at a level of abstraction that doesn't give much away. You can say, "We test for whether the model can meaningfully uplift someone trying to do X," without saying how close the model is or what the specific tasks look like. There's a question of how much detail outsiders need in order to actually hold you accountable, and I think the honest answer is more than developers currently provide but less than full disclosure. Something like a third party who sees the full picture and can say publicly, "Yes, they're following their policy," gets you a lot of the accountability without the hazard.

Where it gets harder is when a threshold actually gets crossed. If your policy says you'll pause or add mitigations at a certain capability level, and then you visibly pause or add mitigations, people can infer you hit the threshold. I think you mostly just have to accept that. The alternative, where you don't tell anyone and quietly change your behavior, undermines the whole point, which is that external parties can verify you're doing what you said. And honestly, the information that some lab has a model that can do something dangerous is much less hazardous than the model itself or the details of how. Knowing that someone crossed a line mostly tells competitors and governments that the line is reachable, and I'd argue that's information society should have.

The last thing I'd say is that I'm fairly skeptical of the "we can't talk about safety because it reveals capabilities" argument in practice. It's sometimes true, but it's also a very convenient thing for a lab to say when it doesn't want scrutiny. So my default is that the burden should be on the developer to explain specifically what would be hazardous to disclose, and to find a mechanism, like a trusted auditor or a government body, for disclosing it to someone, rather than treating secrecy as the baseline.

r001.rationale: It proposes a public commitment to take specified action when capability X is observed, before deploying; that communicates a capability threshold for stronger safeguards.

r002.rationale: The response says to act after observing the threshold and before deployment. It does not say to strengthen protective measures before models reach that threshold.

r003.rationale: It says a developer can publish the conditional commitment before having dangerous capabilities, and commits to safeguards or not deploying if it cannot implement them.

astra-6.text:
I think you can publish the policy in advance, so that it describes what you would do if you encountered various dangerous capabilities, without saying which of those capabilities you currently have. You could say, “If a model could substantially help someone develop a biological weapon, then we would require these safeguards before deploying it.” Publishing that conditional doesn’t imply that you’ve built such a model.

There is a harder question about how people verify that you’re following the policy. You probably want some people outside the company to have access to the relevant evidence, without necessarily making all that evidence public. That could be an auditor or a government agency. They can check whether your safeguards are appropriate without publishing a detailed account of what the model can do.

I don’t think that eliminates all information leakage. If you visibly take some unusual precaution, people may infer something from that. But you can reduce that problem by making commitments early and applying precautions broadly, rather than announcing a new policy every time you discover something concerning.

r001.rationale: It proposes publishing a conditional policy that requires safeguards if a model reaches a stated capability, illustrated by helping develop a biological weapon.

r002.rationale: It says safeguards would be required before deploying a capable model, but does not state that protections can be strengthened before models reach the announced threshold.

r003.rationale: It says the conditional announcement would not imply the developer has built such a model, but does not say the developer is ready to implement the corresponding safeguards before possessing one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you can describe the policy in advance, conditional on what you might observe. You can say, “If a model could meaningfully help someone develop a biological weapon, here are the security measures we would require, and here are the conditions under which we wouldn’t deploy it.” That doesn’t tell you whether any particular model has crossed that threshold.

There is a harder question about how people verify that you’re actually following the policy. You probably want some party who can see the sensitive information and assess whether your precautions are adequate, without publishing all the evidence. That could be a government agency or an independent evaluator.

You can’t necessarily eliminate every bit of information leakage. If you suddenly adopt much stronger security, people may infer something from that. But you can separate being transparent about the rules you’re committing to from being transparent about every capability measurement. The former seems quite valuable even when the latter would be dangerous.

r001.rationale: It proposes stating in advance that if a model could meaningfully help develop a biological weapon, specified security measures would be required.

r002.rationale: It describes announcing requirements in advance, but does not state that the developer can strengthen protections before its models reach the threshold.

r003.rationale: It describes a conditional policy announced in advance, but does not say the developer is prepared to implement those measures before possessing models with the extreme capabilities.
